question: Assume Java 17. Which statement about instance fields that are not explicitly initialized is correct?
options: They receive default values such as 0, false, or null
They must be initialized before the object is created, or compilation fails
Reference-type fields default to an empty object of that type
int fields default to -1 until they are assigned
explanation: Instance fields (and static fields) always get default values: 0 for numeric types, false for boolean, and null for references. Only local variables must be definitely assigned before use.

question: Which statement about a static method accessing instance fields is correct?
options: A static method can read instance fields directly because they belong to the class
A static method cannot use an instance field by simple name; it needs an object reference
A static method can use instance fields only if they are private
A static method can use instance fields only if they are final

It is the name of its class

question: Which statement about a final instance field with no initializer at its declaration is correct?
options: It can be reassigned in any instance method
It must be definitely assigned exactly once by the end of every constructor (or in an initializer block)

question: A BankAccount class must never allow its balance to become negative through withdraw. Which implementation enforces this?

question: Which pair of methods can legally be declared together in the same class?
options: void f(int a) and void f(String a)

options: Always, even when the class declares other constructors
Only when the class declares no constructors of its own

Only when the class is declared public
explanation: The default constructor is generated only if the class has no explicit constructor. Once you declare any constructor, the compiler no longer adds a no-argument one.

question: Which is a valid reason to declare a constructor private?
options: To let subclasses inherit the constructor
To make the object immutable automatically
To prevent instantiation from outside the class, as in a singleton or utility class
explanation: A private constructor can be called only from inside the class. This is used for singletons, utility classes, and static factory methods. It does not make a class abstract or immutable.

question: Which is an advantage of a static factory method over a constructor?
options: It runs faster than a constructor in every case
It can assign final fields without initializing them
It is automatically inherited by subclasses as a constructor
It can return an existing instance or a subtype instead of always creating a new object
explanation: A constructor always creates a new instance of exactly its class. A static factory has a descriptive name and may cache, reuse, or return a subtype. It has no special performance or final-field privileges.

question: Which statement best summarizes how constructors relate to inheritance?
options: Constructors are inherited, so a subclass can be created with any superclass constructor
Constructors are not inherited; each subclass declares its own and chains to a superclass constructor explicitly or implicitly
Constructors are inherited only when they are public
A subclass never needs to run a superclass constructor
explanation: Constructors are not members that get inherited. A subclass constructor must call a superclass constructor, either explicitly with super(...) or implicitly with super().

question: What is the main benefit of using this(...) to chain constructors in the same class?
options: It allows a constructor to return a value
It keeps initialization logic in one place and avoids duplicated code
It lets constructors be inherited by subclasses

question: Which statement best summarizes how a simple name x used inside an instance method is resolved?
options: Local variables and parameters are checked first, then fields of the current class, then inherited fields
Superclass fields are checked first, then the current class, then local variables

question: What is the main purpose of packages in Java?
options: To make a class run faster
To make every class automatically public
To group related classes, avoid name clashes, and support package-level access control
explanation: Packages organize types into namespaces, which avoids naming conflicts and enables the package-private access level. They do not affect speed or make classes public.

question: A field is declared with no access modifier. Which code can access it?
options: Only classes in the same package
explanation: No modifier means package-private (default) access. Only code in the same package can use the member, even if the other class is not a subclass.

question: Which list orders the access levels from most restrictive to least restrictive?
explanation: private allows only the same class, package-private adds the same package, protected adds subclasses in other packages, and public allows everyone.

question: Which statement best describes the rule for the package declaration in a source file?

A file may contain several package statements, one per class
It must be the first statement in the file (comments aside) and appear at most once
It is mandatory for every class, including those in the unnamed package
explanation: A source file has at most one package declaration, placed before any imports and type declarations. If omitted, the classes belong to the unnamed (default) package.

question: Which statement about import java.util.*; is correct?

It imports the types directly in java.util, but not types in its subpackages
It imports every class in the java package tree

question: Why does Main fail to compile?
options: Helper is not public, so it cannot be accessed from package app
Main must be in package util
explanation: A class with no modifier is package-private, so it is visible only inside its own package. Even a public method inside it cannot be reached from another package through the class.

question: Why does Teller fail to compile?
options: balance has package-private access and Teller is in a different package
import bank.Account is invalid because bank is not a real package
explanation: Making the class public only makes the type visible. The field balance has no modifier, so only classes in package bank may access it.

question: Assume Windows Command Prompt (cmd.exe). Compiled classes are in the folder out and a library is lib\util.jar. Which command runs com.shop.App with both on the class path?
explanation: Class path entries are separated by ; on Windows and by : on Linux and macOS. A comma is not a separator, and a space would make lib\util.jar be treated as the main class name.

question: Which code can access a protected member of a class?
options: The same package, plus subclasses even in other packages (subject to the access-through-subclass rule)
Only subclasses that are in the same package
Any class that imports the declaring class
explanation: protected combines package access with access for subclasses in other packages. Importing a class does not grant any extra access.

question: What is the output?
options: Compile-time error because secret is private
explanation: private access is per class, not per object. Code inside Example can read the private field of any Example instance, so the comparison is 3 == 3.

question: A helper method should be callable by classes in the same package only, and by no code outside it, including subclasses elsewhere. Which modifier is correct?
explanation: Package-private is exactly the same-package-only level. protected would also allow subclasses in other packages, and private would block the other classes in the package.

question: What is the output?
options: Compile-time error: static import conflicts with a declared method
explanation: A method declared in the class shadows a statically imported method with the same name. The call resolves to the local max, which returns its first argument, 3.

question: Which line completes Main so that Greeter can be used by its simple name?
explanation: A single-type import names the package and the class. You cannot import a package by itself, import util.Greeter.* imports Greeter's nested types, and a static import must name a member.

question: Why does this code fail to compile?
options: List and ArrayList are in java.util and are not imported
ArrayList cannot be used with List
explanation: Only java.lang is imported automatically. List and ArrayList need import java.util.List and import java.util.ArrayList (or java.util.*), otherwise the compiler reports cannot find symbol.

question: What happens when this code is compiled?
options: Date is not a valid type
It compiles and picks java.util.Date because it is imported first
Compile-time error: reference to Date is ambiguous
explanation: Both java.util and java.sql contain a Date class, and two on-demand imports make the simple name ambiguous. Import order does not matter; use a single-type import or the fully qualified name.

question: Which package declaration is legal?
explanation: Each part of a package name must be a valid identifier. A part cannot start with a digit, be a keyword such as class, or contain a hyphen.

question: A library class Parser in package lib has a method meant to be used by subclasses that users write in other packages, but not by arbitrary unrelated classes outside lib. Which modifier fits best?
explanation: protected allows subclasses in other packages (and the same package) while hiding the member from unrelated outside classes. private would block subclasses, public would open it to everyone, and package-private would block outside subclasses.

question: What happens when Main is compiled?
options: Compile-time error because Base() has protected access in a.Base
It compiles only if Main is declared final
explanation: A protected constructor can be called with new only from inside its own package. Code in another package can reach it only through super(...) from a subclass constructor.

question: What is the output?
options: Compile-time error because x is private in Inner
explanation: Private access is defined by the top-level class body, so the enclosing class can read private members of its nested classes. It prints 4.

question: Assume Linux, the project root as the current directory, and files saved as src/util/Tool.java and src/app/Main.java. Which commands compile and run Main?
options:
javac -d src src/app/Main.java
java -cp src Main

javac -d out src/app/Main.java
java -cp out app.Main

javac -d out -sourcepath src src/app/Main.java
java -cp out app.Main
explanation: javac must be told where to find the other source file, which -sourcepath src does, and -d out places the class files in package folders. The launcher then uses the class path root out and the qualified name app.Main. Without -sourcepath, util.Tool is not found.

question: Which statement best summarizes Java access control?
options: private members are visible to all classes in the same package
Access modifiers decide which code may use a class or member, with private the narrowest and public the widest
Package-private is the widest access level
Access modifiers only affect runtime speed
explanation: Access modifiers control visibility. In order from narrowest to widest: private, package-private, protected, public.

question: What is the output?
options: Compile-time error because who() cannot override
explanation: A package-private method is not inherited by a subclass in a different package, so B.who() does not override it. The call inside A.call() therefore runs A.who().

question: What is a drawback of making instance fields public instead of private?
options: Public fields cannot be read by other packages
Public fields make the class run faster
Public fields let any code change the object's state without validation
Public fields cannot be accessed by subclasses
explanation: Public fields break encapsulation. The class cannot enforce rules on values, and changing the field later can break all code that uses it.

question: Why does this code fail to compile?
options: f must be static in B
An overriding method cannot have weaker access than the method it overrides
explanation: An overriding method may widen but not narrow access. B.f() is package-private while A.f() is public, so the compiler reports that the override attempts to assign weaker access privileges.

question: Use these rules: private = same class only; no modifier = same package only; protected = same package or a subclass; public = everyone. How many of the 8 reads in this pseudocode are permitted?
explanation: B is in the same package but not a subclass, so it can read y, z, and w (3 reads). C is a subclass in another package, so it can read only z and w (2 reads). In total 3 + 2 = 5.
